title: Software Modelling and Model Validation
whyItMatters: Structural analysis software solves the mathematical model you input, not necessarily the real building you intend to build. Every model must be bounded by hand calculations and verified against the 7 mandatory gate questions before any output is trusted.
introduction: Idealising real structures into 1D/2D/3D analytical models, member releases, local axes, support and spring stiffness sensitivity, load combinations, model warnings, and the 7 mandatory validation checks.
objectives: Translate physical structural framing and connections into appropriate 1D/2D/3D elements, local axes, member releases, and boundary restraints.
Configure load cases, combinations, member offsets, floor diaphragm assumptions, and realistic support/rotational spring stiffness bounds.
Interrogate solver warnings (mechanisms, zero-stiffness nodes, ill-conditioned matrices) and verify global equilibrium.
Execute the 7 Mandatory Model Validation Questions on every software model.
learningGate: Never accept a software model without passing all 7 validation questions.

questions.learningObjective: Quantify midspan moment error when a pinned beam is accidentally modelled with fixed ends.
questions.prompt: A 8.0 m simply supported steel beam carries a factored UDL w = 30 kN/m. The true midspan sagging moment (with pinned end releases) is wL^2/8 = 240 kNm. If the modeller forgets to apply end moment releases so the beam is analysed as fully fixed into rigid columns (giving midspan sagging wL^2/24), calculate the midspan sagging moment reported by the flawed software model.
questions.explanation: M_flawed = 30 * 8.0^2 / 24 = 1920 / 24 = 80.0 kNm (underestimating the true midspan moment of 240 kNm by a factor of 3, while transferring 160 kNm hogging into connections not designed for moment!).
questions.citation: BS 5975:2019 Code of Practice for Temporary Works Procedures & Falsework

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a solver instability warning caused by torsional releases.
questions.prompt: In a 3D frame model (6 degrees of freedom per node), the engineer releases both major and minor bending (My, Mz) AND torsion (Mx) at BOTH ends of a secondary beam. The solver reports a "zero stiffness / mechanism warning in Rx". Why?
questions.assumptions: Consider rotational equilibrium of the 1D bar about its own longitudinal x-axis.
options: It redistributes the peak hogging bending moment into the adjacent midspan zone through rigid-plastic hinge rotation without requiring supplementary lateral-torsional restraint, web stiffeners, or ductile rotation capacity at the support interface
Releasing My and Mz deletes the vertical shear stiffness
Releasing torsion Mx at both ends leaves the beam free to spin about its own longitudinal axis like a rolling pin with zero torsional restraint

It eliminates vertical shear deformation across the web depth by forcing the neutral axis to remain coincident with the geometric centroid of the uncracked transformed section throughout both construction and permanent service stages
questions.explanation: A 3D beam element must have torsional rotation Rx restrained at least at one end; releasing Mx at both ends creates a rigid-body rotational mechanism about the member axis.
questions.citation: BS 5975:2019 Code of Practice for Temporary Works Procedures & Falsework
hints: Consider the physical load path, equilibrium boundary conditions, and deformation compatibility for "Diagnose a solver instability warning caused by torsional releases.". Distinguish carefully between ULS strength/stability checks and SLS deflection/cracking behaviour.
Engineering principle check: eliminate options that violate static equilibrium, ignore construction-stage instability, or confuse elastic stiffness (E·I) with material yield strength (f_y).

questions.learningObjective: Identify what a "master-slave rigid floor diaphragm" constraint hides in a 3D frame model.
questions.prompt: When a modeller applies a "rigid horizontal diaphragm" constraint across all nodes of a floor level in a 3D steel frame, what important internal force is automatically suppressed (set to zero) in the beams lying within that floor plane?
questions.assumptions: Consider relative in-plane axial elongation between two nodes locked into a rigid body.
options: Axial tension and compression forces in the floor beams (including wind drag/collector tie forces and thermal restraint forces), because rigid diaphragm nodes cannot move relative to each other in plane
By applying the unfactored characteristic Serviceability Limit State action combination directly to the gross cross-sectional area without accounting for partial material safety factors, seco.
By assuming a uniform linear-elastic stress distribution across the gross flange and web elements while neglecting rotational restraint compatibility, eccentric shear-centre load introduct.
By taking the mean 50th-percentile material stiffness modulus together with a fully fixed rotational boundary condition at both ends, thereby ignoring connection flexibility, long-term.
questions.explanation: A rigid diaphragm locks relative in-plane distance between nodes, meaning floor beams report zero axial force even when acting as wind drag struts or bracing collectors.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why linear superposition of individual load cases is invalid in a tension-only bracing or P-Delta analysis.
questions.prompt: If a 3D model contains tension-only cross-bracing or second-order P-Delta effects, why is it invalid to run Dead, Live, and Wind as separate linear cases and simply add their factored results afterwards?
questions.assumptions: Consider member compression cut-off and stiffness dependence on axial load.
options: Because the maximum principal tensile stress under pure shear equals the uniaxial yield strength according to the Rankine maximum normal stress hypothesis, which governs brittle fracture in unreinforced cast iron and uncracked plain concrete elements rather than ductile structural steel
Because the active structural stiffness matrix changes depending on which braces go slack and how much vertical gravity load P is present simultaneously with lateral drift Delta

Because the elastic shear modulus G is related to Young’s modulus E by G = E / [2(1 + ν)], which introduces a Poisson’s ratio reduction factor across the web depth whenever transverse direct stresses are neglected in simple beam theory
Linear superposition is always exact for buckling and slack cables
questions.explanation: In non-linear (tension-only or P-Delta) analysis, the stiffness depends on the combined load state; full factored combinations must be solved directly.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret finite element stress singularities over point supports in 2D slab meshes.
questions.prompt: In a 2D linear-elastic finite element plate model of a flat slab where columns are modelled as single point supports (pin nodes), what happens to the calculated hogging moment directly at the column node as the mesh size is refined smaller and smaller?
questions.assumptions: Recall the theoretical elasticity solution over a zero-area point support.
options: It redistributes the peak hogging bending moment into the adjacent midspan zone through rigid-plastic hinge rotation without requiring supplementary lateral-torsional restraint, web stiffeners, or ductile rotation capacity at the support interface

It increases the elastic Euler critical buckling load by halving the effective buckling length between inflection points, provided that the connection detail transfers full axial thrust without slip or local web crippling

The elastic peak moment at the zero-area point node tends toward infinity (a mathematical singularity); practical design integrates moments over a realistic strip width or models the finite column/drop size

It eliminates vertical shear deformation across the web depth by forcing the neutral axis to remain coincident with the geometric centroid of the uncracked transformed section throughout both construction and permanent service stages

questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a wildly unrealistic software deflection (e.g. 42,000 mm on a 6 m beam).
questions.prompt: A 6 m steel beam in a frame model reports a vertical deflection of 42,500 mm (42.5 metres!) without crashing the solver. What is the most likely cause?
questions.assumptions: Consider near-mechanisms or unit mismatch in input parameters.
options: Because the maximum principal tensile stress under pure shear equals the uniaxial yield strength according to the Rankine maximum normal stress hypothesis, which governs brittle fracture in unreinforced cast iron and uncracked plain concrete elements rather than ductile structural steel
A partial mechanism (such as an unrestrained pin/roller or collinear internal hinges restrained only by tiny numerical dummy stiffness) or a gross units error in E, I, or load

Because the elastic shear modulus G is related to Young’s modulus E by G = E / [2(1 + ν)], which introduces a Poisson’s ratio reduction factor across the web depth whenever transverse direct stresses are neglected in simple beam theory

Because Eurocode partial safety factors for resistance incorporate a statistical log-normal coefficient of variation for hot-rolled plate thickness tolerances, mill rolling residual stresses, and out-of-straightness bow imperfections across the member length
questions.explanation: Displacements of metres or kilometres in a linear elastic solver indicate either a near-mechanism (stabilised only by solver spring tolerance) or a 10^3 / 10^6 unit error.
